Overview

Liechtenstein at a Glance

Liechtenstein is a constitutional monarchy of about 41,000 people with a civil law tradition, a customs and currency union with Switzerland, and membership of the European Economic Area since 1995. EEA membership brings EU data protection and anti-money laundering standards into national law, and the financial sector is supervised by the Financial Market Authority. The Office of Justice maintains the commercial register, the land register and the register of beneficial owners. For investigators, the defining feature is the large number of foundations, establishments and trusts administered by licensed fiduciaries, many for non-residents, which hold assets and controlling interests in entities chartered elsewhere.

Organisations commission investigative work involving Liechtenstein mostly because a structure registered in Vaduz sits somewhere in a chain of ownership or a flow of funds. Typical matters include tracing assets in divorce, inheritance and insolvency proceedings, identifying who controls a foundation that holds shares or property abroad, and supporting fraud and recovery claims where proceeds passed through Liechtenstein entities. Corporate acquirers and lenders also review ownership chains that include Liechtenstein vehicles. The country is also a significant industrial location, home to manufacturers of tools, dental products and precision instruments, which leads to ordinary supply-chain and counterparty checks.

Law & Regulation

What applies before any work touching Liechtenstein begins

Legal system

Liechtenstein has a civil law system drawing on Austrian and Swiss law, with its own legislation on persons and companies governing foundations, establishments and trusts. Ordinary jurisdiction lies with the Regional Court (Landgericht) in Vaduz at first instance, the Princely High Court of Appeal at second instance and the Princely Supreme Court as the final appellate court. An Administrative Court and a Constitutional Court (Staatsgerichtshof) complete the structure. Commercial and foundation disputes, including supervisory proceedings over foundations, are heard by the ordinary courts, and the country is a member of the EEA and EFTA.

Data protection

General Data Protection Regulation (EU) 2016/679, applicable through the EEA Agreement, and the Data Protection Act (Datenschutzgesetz, DSG) of 4 October 2018 · Regulator: Datenschutzstelle Fürstentum Liechtenstein (Data Protection Authority), Vaduz

As an EEA state, Liechtenstein applies the GDPR, supplemented by the Data Protection Act of 2018. Investigative work involving personal data requires a lawful basis, most often legitimate interests supported by a documented balancing test, together with transparency, minimisation and storage limits. Criminal-offence data is tightly restricted. The Datenschutzstelle receives notifications of video surveillance, which indicates scrutiny of camera use. Transfers to the United States and other third countries must meet GDPR Chapter V requirements, such as adequacy, including the EU-US Data Privacy Framework for certified recipients, or standard contractual clauses.

Private investigators

We have not confirmed from an official source whether private detective work is a licensed trade in Liechtenstein; the trade legislation we located has been revised and its current treatment of investigative services could not be verified. Engagements are therefore scoped with Liechtenstein counsel. Whatever the licensing position, strict limits apply. The GDPR and the Data Protection Act govern any collection of personal data, video surveillance is subject to notification, and banking and professional secrecy obligations of banks, fiduciaries and lawyers mean that client and account information is not available to private parties. Information about foundations is often obtainable only through court or authority proceedings.

Corporate & public records

The commercial register is kept by the Office of Justice and offers a company index, extracts and public access to registered information, with some limitations of disclosure. Many foundations are only deposited rather than registered, so their details are not publicly visible. The Office of Justice also maintains the register of beneficial owners (VwbP) under its foundation supervision and anti-money laundering unit, alongside a central register of accounts; access to beneficial ownership data is restricted rather than generally public, and Open Ownership lists Liechtenstein as planning further transparency measures. The land register, also kept by the Office of Justice, records property ownership.

Anti-corruption & AML

Bribery and corruption offences are set out in the Criminal Code, which follows the Austrian model, and are prosecuted by the Office of the Public Prosecutor. Anti-money laundering obligations derive from the Due Diligence Act (Sorgfaltspflichtgesetz, SPG) of 11 December 2008, supervised by the Financial Market Authority, which oversees banks, fiduciaries and other intermediaries. The Financial Intelligence Unit receives suspicious activity reports through goAML. MONEYVAL adopted its fifth-round evaluation of Liechtenstein in May 2022.

General information compiled 2026-11-04 from the sources listed below. It is not legal advice; TDSC works with qualified local counsel on questions of law.

Engagement Standard

How TDSC Scopes Matters Touching Liechtenstein

TDSC treats most Liechtenstein matters as cross-border structure research. Engagements begin with a jurisdictional review of what the client is entitled to obtain, which in Liechtenstein often depends on court proceedings, standing as a beneficiary or creditor, or authority cooperation rather than on investigative inquiries. TDSC then maps what a structure holds and who is connected to it from commercial register extracts, foreign registries, property and court records and German-language sources, and identifies where Liechtenstein counsel should seek disclosure. TDSC does not attempt to obtain bank, fiduciary or beneficial ownership register data outside lawful channels. Personal data is processed under GDPR principles, with transfers to the United States documented under Chapter V.

TDSC has no office in Liechtenstein. Engagements are directed from Nashville, Tennessee; where work on the ground is needed, it is performed by appropriately licensed local professionals under a written scope. TDSC does not provide legal advice.

Typical Matters

Where Investigative Work Involving Liechtenstein Concentrates

01

Foundation and trust asset tracing

Identifying assets held through Liechtenstein foundations, establishments and trusts in divorce, inheritance, insolvency and fraud matters, by mapping what those structures own abroad through foreign registries, property records and filings, and preparing evidence counsel can use to seek disclosure through the Liechtenstein courts.

02

Ownership chain research

Tracing ownership chains that pass through Liechtenstein vehicles for acquirers, lenders and compliance teams, combining commercial register extracts, foreign corporate records, annual reports and litigation to identify likely controllers where beneficial ownership data is not publicly accessible.

03

Fiduciary and intermediary background

Reviewing the history and reputation of Vaduz fiduciaries, directors and protectors connected to a structure, including disciplinary or supervisory actions, litigation and media coverage, to help clients assess governance risk and the reliability of information provided by intermediaries.

04

Cross-border fraud support

Supporting victims and their counsel where proceeds of fraud passed through Liechtenstein entities or banks, by reconstructing the external picture of transactions and parties from public and lawfully obtained sources, to support criminal complaints, freezing applications or mutual legal assistance requests by counsel.

05

Industrial counterparty due diligence

Background checks on Liechtenstein manufacturers, suppliers and their owners for procurement, distribution and acquisition decisions, covering registered officers, ownership, litigation, insolvency notices and reputation in German-language media across Liechtenstein, Switzerland and Austria.

Questions

Liechtenstein: Frequently Asked Questions

Can you find out who is behind a Liechtenstein foundation?

Sometimes, but rarely from Liechtenstein records alone. Many foundations are deposited rather than registered, and beneficial ownership data is not generally public. TDSC works outward from what the foundation owns, who administers it and where it appears in foreign records and litigation, and helps counsel decide whether to seek disclosure through the courts.

Does the GDPR apply to investigations involving Liechtenstein?

Yes. Liechtenstein applies the GDPR through the EEA Agreement, supplemented by its Data Protection Act of 2018, supervised by the Datenschutzstelle. TDSC documents a lawful basis for each inquiry, keeps data to what the matter needs, and uses an approved Chapter V mechanism when data is transferred to the United States.

Can TDSC obtain bank information from Liechtenstein?

No. Bank and fiduciary information is protected by secrecy and data protection rules and is not available to private investigators. Access comes through court orders, insolvency administrators or mutual legal assistance. TDSC can support those routes by assembling the external evidence that justifies an application, which counsel then pursues.

Which court hears disputes over a Liechtenstein foundation?

Foundation disputes and supervisory matters are heard by the ordinary courts, beginning with the Regional Court in Vaduz, with appeals to the Princely High Court of Appeal and the Princely Supreme Court. TDSC does not advise on procedure, but supports Liechtenstein counsel with factual research on assets and parties.

Is Liechtenstein still considered high-risk for money laundering?

Liechtenstein has tightened its framework significantly since the late 2000s. The Due Diligence Act of 2008, supervision by the Financial Market Authority and a financial intelligence unit are in place, and MONEYVAL completed a fifth-round evaluation in 2022. TDSC assesses each structure on its own facts rather than relying on the jurisdiction's historical reputation.
